business_problem: DXC wanted to reduce the cost and complexity of data engineering for its own SaaS applications and global clients while bringing AI and vector-search capabilities closer to data already spread across multicloud and hybrid environments.
solution_summary: DXC migrated parts of its SaaS and client-facing data architecture onto Oracle Autonomous Database and Oracle Autonomous Transaction Processing on OCI so structured, unstructured, and real-time data could be consolidated without heavy custom engineering. The platform supports separate development, test, and production environments for DXC's International Material Data Systems SaaS offering and provides AI capabilities from Oracle Database 23ai, including vector-search functionality the company is exploring for chatbot-based support. Because Oracle Database can work with open source or proprietary language models and interact with data without copying it into separate AI stores, DXC sees it as a simpler platform for customers with compliance-sensitive workloads. The Oracle stack lets DXC modernize application data flows, lower operating cost relative to its prior environment, and create a base for semantic search and AI automation across software and consulting engagements.

data_flow: Application data from DXC's SaaS environments and client workloads is consolidated into Oracle Autonomous Database and Autonomous Transaction Processing on OCI, where Oracle Database AI features operate directly on existing data to support insights, semantic search, and planned chatbot experiences without extra copying.
business_outcome: DXC simplified data engineering, lowered the cost of running separate SaaS environments, and created a platform for semantic search and AI automation that it can reuse in both its own software offerings and client modernization work.
